- hyperframes: Mandatory entry point: read this first for any request to make, create, edit, animate, or render a video, animation, or motion graphic, including a promo, explainer, captioned clip, title card, overlay, slideshow or interactive deck, Remotion port, or any HyperFrames HTML composition. Also use it to inspect, diagnose, validate, preview, publish, or batch-render an existing HyperFrames project. Inputs may be a website URL, GitHub PR, Figma design or URL, text or brief, existing footage, or music. It resumes project state, captures intent when applicable, selects and installs the owning workflow, and routes domain capabilities. HyperFrames is the default output framework unless the user explicitly chooses another framework for the deliverable or asks only to record a browser session.
- hyperframes-animation: All animation knowledge for HyperFrames — atomic motion rules, multi-phase scene blueprints, scene transitions, broader motion-design techniques, AND the seven runtime adapters (GSAP default, plus Lottie, Three.js, Anime.js, CSS keyframes, Web Animations API, TypeGPU). Use for any motion or animation task: pick 2-4 rules and compose, or load a blueprint, or look up runtime-specific API (e.g. GSAP eases / Lottie player / Three.js mixer). Also covers auditing an existing composition's choreography (animation map) and 24 named text-animation effects. HyperFrames-native: single paused timeline, seek-safe, deterministic.
- hyperframes-cli: Use the HyperFrames CLI development loop: init, add, catalog, capture, lint, check, snapshot, compare, grade-compare, preview, play, present, beats, keyframes, single or batch render, publish, cloud, cloudrun, feedback, lambda, doctor, browser, info, upgrade, skills, compositions, docs, benchmark, telemetry, transcribe, auth, tts, and remove-background. Also use when diagnosing build or render failures. validate, inspect, and layout are deprecated aliases; use check. Covers local, HeyGen-hosted cloud, AWS Lambda, and Google Cloud Run rendering.
- hyperframes-core: The HyperFrames composition contract — build one renderable project. Use for composition structure, the `data-*` timing attributes, `class="clip"`, tracks, sub-compositions, variables, framework-owned media playback, deterministic-render rules, and validation. Also covers Tailwind projects and the STORYBOARD.md / SCRIPT.md plan formats. Read before writing composition HTML.
- hyperframes-creative: Non-animation creative direction for HyperFrames videos. Use for design spec (frame.md / design.md) handling, palettes, typography, narration, beat planning, audio-reactive visuals, composition patterns, and brand / style decisions. For atomic motion patterns and scene blueprints, use `hyperframes-animation`.
- hyperframes-keyframes: Use when a HyperFrames composition needs seek-safe 2D/3D keyframes, GSAP timelines, CSS keyframes, Anime.js, WAAPI, FLIP, paths, masks, SVG morph/draw, text trails, 3D depth, or `hyperframes keyframes` diagnostics. Don't use for broad scene strategy, brand design, media sourcing, captions, or general video planning.
- hyperframes-registry: Install, discover, and wire registry blocks and components into HyperFrames compositions. Use when running hyperframes add or hyperframes catalog, installing one item or every block matching a tag, wiring an installed item into index.html, or working with hyperframes.json. Covers discovery, install locations, block sub-composition wiring, component snippet merging, and authoring a new block or component to contribute upstream (idea → scaffold → validate → PR).
- media-use: Agent Media OS, the single skill for every media need in a HyperFrames project. Resolve BGM, SFX, image, icon, brand logo, voice, color grade, or LUT into a frozen local file or paste-ready block + ledger record (one verb, `resolve`); generate via TTS / music / image models when the catalog misses; produce voiceover, transcription, captions, and background removal through one shared audio engine; operate on media (cut / reframe / transform); and reuse assets across projects. Keeps search noise on disk, hands the agent one path or block. Use for any audio, image, icon, logo, voiceover, caption, color-grading, or media-asset need.

Copy the input `_task` unchanged to the top level of the output. `title` must exactly match the input source title.

Return structured facts, not newsletter prose:

- `event_hint`: short event identity.
- `problem`: concrete problem addressed.
- `mechanism`: distinguishing design/mechanism.
- `evidence`: 0-5 strongest records already supported by the visible Evidence Pack. Keep material baseline/condition for every number and a precise section/page/figure/table/heading locator.
- `evaluation_context`: workload, scale, hardware/software, baseline, or deployment context that is actually visible.

Each gap needs a concrete `question` and 1-8 source-native literal `terms` (system/baseline/hardware/metric/table/workload names) for deterministic retrieval. Never request later text merely for completeness.

Treat abstract/introduction performance claims as **claims**, not fully verified experiment facts, when the visible front evidence omits their baseline or material conditions. In that case either weaken the claim or request the specific missing evidence through `evidence_gaps`; the one-shot repair stage will search only the unread suffix of the same primary source.

11	    "summary": "Disaggregated LLM serving runs prefill and decode on separate GPU pools to keep the two phases from interfering. In practice, this creates a new asymmetry: under bursty, heavy-tailed workloads prefill nodes saturate while decode nodes have compute underutilized, and on a production-style A100 cluster with 2 prefill and 2 decode nodes (2P2D), we find that prefill execution accounts for only 2-23% of P95 Time-to-First-Token (TTFT). Queuing and inter-node GPU-GPU KV-cache transfer account for the rest. We present a proactive prefill-deflecting scheduler that lets decode nodes serve prefill phase of requests as chunked-prefill steps interleaved with their in-flight decode batches. For each queued request, we estimate the TTFT it would see on the prefill node, and on every decode node, search for the largest chunk schedule that keeps in-flight decodes within their Time-Between-Tokens (TBT) SLO and deflect when the decode path helps tail latency. Because the prefill phase of deflected requests runs in place on the decode node, the inter-node KV transfer is eliminated. Implemented on vLLM and evaluated on production-style traces with DeepSeek-V2-Lite, our approach reduces P95 TTFT by upto 81% and raises SLO attainment by upto 79% over state-of-the-art disaggregated schedulers, at sub-millisecond per-request routing cost.",

In practice, this creates a new asymmetry: under bursty, heavy-tailed workloads prefill nodes saturate while decode nodes have compute underutilized, and on a production-style A100 cluster with 2 prefill and 2 decode nodes (2P2D), we find that prefill execution accounts for only 2-23% of P95 Time-to-First-Token (TTFT). Queuing and inter-node GPU-GPU KV-cache transfer account for the rest. We present a proactive prefill-deflecting scheduler that lets decode nodes serve prefill phase of requests as chunked-prefill steps interleaved with their in-flight decode batches. For each queued request, we estimate the TTFT it would see on the prefill node, and on every decode node, search for the largest chunk schedule that keeps in-flight decodes within their Time-Between-Tokens (TBT) SLO and deflect when the decode path helps tail latency. Because the prefill phase of deflected requests runs in place on the decode node, the inter-node KV transfer is eliminated. Implemented on vLLM and evaluated on production-style traces with DeepSeek-V2-Lite, our approach reduces P95 TTFT by upto 81% and raises SLO attainment by upto 79% over state-of-the-art disaggregated schedulers, at sub-millisecond per-request routing cost.",

11	    "summary": "KV cache compression is essential for efficient long-context inference. Existing eviction methods permanently discard unselected tokens and consequently remove their aggregate contribution to attention. Merging-based alternatives preserve more information but can perturb retained keys and values that should remain exact. We observe that the information omitted by cache eviction can be formulated as residual statistics in both the numerator and denominator of softmax attention. Based on this observation, we propose ResKV, which divides a fixed KV budget into an exact main cache and a compact residual cache that reconstructs the contribution of omitted tokens. ResKV lets main-cache tokens and residual entries participate in the same softmax normalization, so residual entries restore both attention numerator and denominator mass rather than acting as a post-hoc correction. A construction-time validation proxy determines residual allocation for each layer and KV head, while a decode-time dynamic gate adjusts residual contributions for individual queries. Comprehensive evaluations on LongBench and RULER, covering query-aware and query-agnostic settings, multiple backbones, cache budgets, and representative compression baselines, demonstrate broad improvements under the same retained KV budget while preserving the practical efficiency of compressed decoding, including peak memory usage and long-context decode throughput.",

10	    "title": "SeDeM: Selective Decompression of Hidden-State Memories for Long-Context Question Answering",
11	    "summary": "Long-context inference with large language models (LLMs) is costly: self-attention during prefill scales quadratically with sequence length, and the key-value (KV) cache grows with the number of processed tokens. Larger context windows also do not ensure reliable evidence use. Context compression reduces this cost, but many soft-compression methods use LLMs as compressors and rely on compact memory tokens both to preserve information and to condition the decoder. We propose SeDeM, a selective decompression framework that decouples compact memory storage from decoder conditioning. An LLM extracts hidden states from a chosen intermediate Transformer layer, a lightweight compressor stores them as memory blocks, a query-conditioned selector selects relevant blocks, and a decompressor expands only the selected blocks into hidden states compatible with an intermediate decoder layer. Thus, the decoder avoids both full-context processing and direct generation from highly compressed memory slots.     "title": "SeDeM: Selective Decompression of Hidden-State Memories for Long-Context Question Answering",
    "summary": "Long-context inference with large language models (LLMs) is costly: self-attention during prefill scales quadratically with sequence length, and the key-value (KV) cache grows with the number of processed tokens. Larger context windows also do not ensure reliable evidence use. Context compression reduces this cost, but many soft-compression methods use LLMs as compressors and rely on compact memory tokens both to preserve information and to condition the decoder. We propose SeDeM, a selective decompression framework that decouples compact memory storage from decoder conditioning. An LLM extracts hidden states from a chosen intermediate Transformer layer, a lightweight compressor stores them as memory blocks, a query-conditioned selector selects relevant blocks, and a decompressor expands only the selected blocks into hidden states compatible with an intermediate decoder layer. Thus, the decoder avoids both full-context processing and direct generation from highly compressed memory slots. On four long-context QA benchmarks, SeDeM achieves higher QA scores than the evaluated compression baselines in both 1B and 3B same-backbone settings, and with the 3B backbone exceeds full-context fine-tuning on three datasets. The learned selector uses block-level evidence supervision during training. SeDeM also reduces online time-to-first-token and improves autoregressive decoding throughput relative to ICAE.",

11	    "summary": "Modern LLM infrastructure increasingly manages tensors not only as computation data, but also as persistent states shared across distributed components. Existing systems optimize individual tensor management tasks, such as model weight loading, KV cache management, and checkpoint synchronization, by deeply integrating task-specific mechanisms with execution engines, networks, or storage backends. However, this specialization creates isolated silos that hinder the reuse and composition of tensor management strategies across evolving LLM workloads. In this paper, we identify tensor lifecycle management as a missing abstraction layer in LLM infrastructure and propose Tensor-as-a-Service (TaaS), which decouples tensor state management from computation logic. We design and build TensorCast, a distributed tensor management layer that provides first-class tensor abstractions, programmable lifecycle primitives, and a runtime that separates tensor management policies from execution mechanisms. This enables developers to write tensor management programs using TensorCast APIs while transparently leveraging distributed execution and data movement. We integrate TensorCast with vLLM and SGLang and evaluate it across diverse tensor lifecycle workloads, including model weight materialization, weight synchronization, KV cache management, and programmable request routing. Our results show that TensorCast achieves competitive performance with specialized tensor management systems while enabling new cross-component optimization policies. A programmable policy implemented with TensorCast improves median TTFT by up to 93.2% under highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads.",

9	Deep Agentic Search for Repository-Level Code
10	Question Answering: An Empirical Study
11	Amirkia Rafiei Oskooei·Bora Ilci·
12	Alperen Kayim·Mehmet Egemen
13	Uzun·Berat Can·Kaan Emre Kara·
14	Ozan Orhan·Mehmet S. Aktas
15	AbstractCode agents spend much of their effort simply locating the right
16	code inside a repository. Two approaches dominate current practice. In Seman-
17	tic Search, the agent retrieves code blocks from a vector index built from the
18	repository in advance. In Deep Agentic Search (also known as grep-search by
19	subagent), a planning agent delegates the exploration to a separate subagent
20	that works in an isolated context window and returns only a condensed result.
21	The second design, which is considered good context engineering practice, ex-
22	ists to protect the main agent from context pollution (also known as context
23	rot), the loss of accuracy that occurs as unrelated material accumulates in
24	the context window. Recent code agents (such as Claude Code, Codex, Anti-
25	gravity, etc) have adopted it quickly, but there is little evidence on whether
26	it produces better answers. We compare the two approaches on SWE-QA, a
27	benchmark for repository-level code question answering. Semantic search an-
28	swered 65.2% of questions correctly against 46.2% for deep agentic search, and
29	it produced each correct answer at less than half the cost. To explain the gap,
30	we then coded every failed run into a taxonomy of failure modes. The taxon-
31	omy shows that deep agentic search did not remove failures but introduced a
32	new class of them: the single largest share of its failures, 41.8%, occurred at
33	the hand-off between the planner and its sub-agent, and these were usually
34	silent, ending in a fluent and confident answer that was wrong. Deep agentic
35	search addresses a real problem and is now the preferred design in many code

53	Deep Agentic Search for Repo-Level Code QA 3
54	1 Introduction
55	Large language models have turned code agents into a primary interface for
56	software development. Developers increasingly write, understand, debug, and
57	maintain software through these agents, whether inside an integrated devel-
58	opment environment or at the command line. One task recurs throughout this
59	workflow, namely code question answering, which is the task of answering a
60	natural language question about a codebase. A question can concern a single
61	function, class, or snippet, or it can concern an entire repository.

89	setting with multiple-choice questions (Elkoussy and Perez, 2026) and with

91	SWE-QA refers to the benchmark of Peng et al. (2026a), which is the dataset
92	we evaluate on. CoReQA (Chen et al., 2025) and CodeRepoQA (Hu et al.,
93	2025) build repository-level question sets from issue threads and maintainer
94	dialogues, and StackRepoQA (Alebachew et al., 2026) draws repository ques-
95	tions from community answers, while LongCodeBench (Rando et al., 2025)
96	instead stresses very long context windows. These benchmarks fix the task and

100	agents, not against a hierarchical agent, and they report accuracy rather than

110	mirrors how command-line assistants offload exploration to a smaller explorer
111	agent, and it is distinct from the flat single agents used in the prior comparisons
112	above. We further accompany the accuracy comparison with three analyses
113	that prior work reports at most in part: a cost and efficiency analysis in tokens
114	and dollars that includes the cost per correct answer, an analysis of agent
115	behaviour through tool use and trajectory length, and a systematic taxonomy
116	of failure modes. The combination of the Deep Agentic search paradigm with
117	these three analyses, across four language models on a shared benchmark, is
118	what distinguishes our study from the work reviewed above.
119	4 Experimental Design
120	This empirical study was conducted as a collaborative research effort between
121	Intellica Business Intelligence and researchers at Yildiz Technical University.
122	We compare two agent architectures, a ReAct agent that uses Semantic search
123	and a Deep Agent that uses Deep Agentic search. Each question is answered
124	in a fresh conversation thread, so that no question can contaminate another,
125	and only the repository targeted by the question is available to the agent. All

Deep Agentic Search for Repository-Level Code
Question Answering: An Empirical Study

Ozan Orhan·Mehmet S. Aktas
AbstractCode agents spend much of their effort simply locating the right
code inside a repository. Two approaches dominate current practice. In Seman-
tic Search, the agent retrieves code blocks from a vector index built from the
repository in advance. In Deep Agentic Search (also known as grep-search by
subagent), a planning agent delegates the exploration to a separate subagent
that works in an isolated context window and returns only a condensed result.
The second design, which is considered good context engineering practice, ex-
ists to protect the main agent from context pollution (also known as context
rot), the loss of accuracy that occurs as unrelated material accumulates in
the context window. Recent code agents (such as Claude Code, Codex, Anti-
gravity, etc) have adopted it quickly, but there is little evidence on whether
it produces better answers. We compare the two approaches on SWE-QA, a
benchmark for repository-level code question answering. Semantic search an-
swered 65.2% of questions correctly against 46.2% for deep agentic search, and
it produced each correct answer at less than half the cost. To explain the gap,
we then coded every failed run into a taxonomy of failure modes. The taxon-
omy shows that deep agentic search did not remove failures but introduced a
new class of them: the single largest share of its failures, 41.8%, occurred at
the hand-off between the planner and its sub-agent, and these were usually
silent, ending in a fluent and confident answer that was wrong. Deep agentic
search addresses a real problem and is now the preferred design in many code

263	Modern LLM inference splits each request into two compu-

265	Prefillprocesses the full input prompt in a single forward

267	It iscompute-bound, and its duration scales primarily with
268	prompt length. The output of the prefill is the KV cache
269	(key/value activations for every layer and token) plus the
270	first generated token.

272	per forward pass, attending over all previously generated
273	tokens. It ismemory-bandwidthbound: each step reads the
274	full KV cache but performs little new compute. Per-step
275	latency typically depends on batch size and aggregate KV-
276	cache size.

278	long and memory-intensive. Running both on the same GPU
279	forces them to share resources that they each under use,
280	which is the basic motivation for disaggregated serving.

(HPLD), retrieval augmented summarization (HPHD) and let
us isolate the effect of each phase on cluster behavior.
Unless noted, all experiments use the cluster described in

80 GB.1

From §2, we know that prefill is compute-bound and de-
code is memory-bandwidth-bound. We measure the extent
to which this difference is exhibited across the different work-

We run each workload of Table 1 to steady state on the

ble 2) and (ii) per-request P95 TTFT breakdown into prefill
queue wait, prefill execution, KV-cache transfer, and decode
queue wait (Table 3).

ated by some workloads.Across every workload, prefill
SM utilization is 75-84% while decode SM utilization never
exceeds 27%. Within that pattern, both sides show a mild but
consistent workload dependence. On the prefill side, long-
prompt workloads (HPLD, HPHD) push SM utilization to
83-84% compared to the 75-76% of short-prompt workloads
because the per-step GEMMs grow with sequence length
and operate closer to roofline. On the decode side, SM uti-
lization tracks the concurrent decode batch size and cache
length: LPHD with short prefills feeding long decodes at a
high RPS sustains the most simultaneous decode streams and
reaches 26% SM utilization, while HPLD with long prefills

given an incoming request, can we deflect it to a decode node

Answering this question requires three pieces of information
that are all computable at scheduling time: (1) the expected
TTFT if the request stays on the prefill node, given current
queue depth and request order, (2) the time to complete prefill
phase of the request on decode node for a sequence of safe

Kairos: time-aware prefill deflection.We present
Kairos, a proactive scheduling framework for disaggregated
LLM serving that reroutes prefill phase of requests to decode
nodes when doing so improves tail TTFT without violat-
ing TBT SLO. For each request in the prefill phase,Kairos
estimates its TTFT under the current prefill schedule. Con-
currently, for every decode node in the cluster, it sweeps
over a set of candidate chunk size sequence (chunk sizes for
each step of the prefill phase) and models resulting per-step
latency. For each (node, chunk size sequence) pair,Kairos
checks two conditions: (i) TBT safety: does adding a chun-
ked prefill to the decode node’s batch increase any in-flight
decode request’s step latency beyond its TBT SLO? and (ii)
TTFT effect: is the projected TTFT for serving a request on
the decode node less than 𝛼 times the projected TTFT on the
prefill node? If both conditions hold,Kairosdeflects prefill
phase of a request to the decode node and executes it at a
specific chunk-size schedule as decided byKairos; other-
wise the request gets routed to a prefill node. The parameter
𝛼≥ 1is a single operator-tunable knob: 𝛼= 1deflects only
when the decode path is strictly faster while 𝛼> 1permits
a bounded TTFT regression for the deflected request when
doing so relieves the prefill queue for requests behind it (all
within the request’s own TTFT SLO). The design requires
only one-time deployment-time profiling, no changes to the
model, and a light per-request scheduling computation at
the prefill dispatcher.
ContributionsThis paper makes the following contribu-
tions:
• A motivating characterization of prefill-node bot-
tlenecks(§3). We show on a normalized production
trace that under bursty arrival patterns, prefill queuing
and KV cache transfer dominates P95 TTFT even at
moderate load, while decode nodes carry spare com-
pute capacity. We also show that static policies based
on thresholds leave performance on the table.
• A TBT safety model for mixed prefill-decode batches
(§4). We derive an analytical model that predicts per-
step latency on a decode node as a function of in-flight
decode batch size, KV cache occupancy, and added
prefill chunk size. This model enables the chunk-size
sweep at low cost and without live inference trials.
• A time-aware deflection decision algorithm(§4).
For each request in the prefill phase,Kairos(i) esti-
mates TTFT on the prefill node, (ii) sweeps (decode
node, chunk size schedule) pairs to find TBT-safe con-
figurations, and (iii) deflects if the best decode-node
TTFT is below𝛼times the prefill-node TTFT.
• A full system implementation on vLLM(§5).Kairos
is implemented on top of vLLM 0.18.1 [8] with approx-

scheduling overhead is less than 1 ms.
• An evaluation(§6) on production derived trace from
Company X, showing P95 TTFT improvement of upto
81%, and upto 79% higher SLO attainment under bursty
load compared to state-of-the-art disaggregated sched-
ulers.
Code forKairosis available at
https://github.com/sudokara/Kairos.
2 Background
2.1 LLM Inference: Prefill and Decode
Modern LLM inference splits each request into two compu-
tational phases with very different resource profiles.
Prefillprocesses the full input prompt in a single forward
pass, computing attention over all input tokens in parallel.
It iscompute-bound, and its duration scales primarily with
prompt length. The output of the prefill is the KV cache
(key/value activations for every layer and token) plus the
first generated token.
Decodegenerates output tokens autoregressively, one
per forward pass, attending over all previously generated
tokens. It ismemory-bandwidthbound: each step reads the
full KV cache but performs little new compute. Per-step
latency typically depends on batch size and aggregate KV-
cache size.
Prefill is short and compute-intensive while decode is
long and memory-intensive. Running both on the same GPU
forces them to share resources that they each under use,
which is the basic motivation for disaggregated serving.
2.2 Disaggregated Serving
Disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on dedicated
GPU node pools, transferring the KV between instances
when a request transitions from prefill to decode. The canon-
ical designs Splitwise [15], DistServe [21], Mooncake [16],
and TetriInfer [6] differ in placement policy, KV-cache man-
agement, and hardware heterogeneity, but all share the as-
sumption that a request that arrives at a prefill node stays
there until prefill completes, after which its KV cache is
shipped to a decode node.

50	1 Introduction
51	Modern LLM coding agents—general-purpose as-
52	sistants like Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025) and
53	open GitHub-issue-solving frameworks like Open-
54	Hands (Wang et al., 2024)—share a common in-
55	efficiency in how they allocate their token budget:
56	much of it is spentfindingthe file to patch, not writ-
57	ing the patch itself. In this work, we ground this
58	observation on a concrete instance: a 30B Open-
59	Hands agent on SWE-Bench Verified (Jimenez
60	et al., 2023) averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens
61	per resolved issue, with a large fraction consumed
62	bygrep,glob, andview_file calls issued in am-
63	biguous exploration loops—often 20+ rounds in a
64	wrong direction before the agent gives up.
65	Can a specialized retrieval submodule shorten
66	this exploration phase? Two hypotheses have not
67	been jointly tested.H1 (effectiveness): better file-
68	level retrieval steers the agent past dead-end ex-
69	plorations and raises the resolve rate.H2 (effi-
70	ciency): the agent resolves roughly the same set
71	of issues but with a shorter rollout. Distinguish-
72	ing them requires evaluating a retriever both on
73	its intrinsic quality and on its downstream effect
74	within the same agent stack—a comparison ab-
75	sent from prior open code retrievers, from lexical
76	(BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009)) to static
77	dense encoders (Feng et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2021;

This first read intentionally spans problem context, mechanism, evaluation/results, and limitations. Evidence locators preserve the source section names.

CodeGrep: An RL-Trained Retrieval Agent for LLM Coding Agents
Wuya Chen1,∗ and Yihao Yang2 and Yang Cao2 and Yue Lin1
{chenwuya@corp.netease.com, 13590078189@163.com}
{yihao786, cy1835208239}@gmail.com
gzlinyue@corp.netease.com
1Netease Guangzhou AI Lab 2Independent Researcher
Abstract
Modern LLM coding agents—Claude Code,
OpenHands—share a common inefficiency:
they spend most of their token budgetfinding
the file to patch, not patching it. On SWE-
Bench Verified, a30B OpenHands agent aver-
ages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved is-
sue, dominated bygrep,glob, andview_file
calls. No open, systematically-studied agent-
style code retriever exists at scale to shorten
this phase. We introduceCodeGrep, a 14B re-
trievalagenttrained end-to-end with GRPO to
issue multi-turn parallel grep/glob/read tool
calls and return candidate files to a frozen down-
stream coding agent.
On all 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances,
CodeGrep delivers a small but reproducibly
positive resolve-rate lift ( +1.2pp: 25.8%→
27.0%) alongside a much larger efficiency
gain (−15% rounds, −19% tokens on resolved
instances). Across three retrievers, down-
stream utility follows aprecision threshold:
BM25 (precision 0.375) degrades the agent,
Jina ( 0.445) is neutral, and only CodeGrep
(0.677) crosses the threshold at which retrieval
begins to buy efficiency. To enable this study,
we mine supervision from 67K open-source
agent trajectories (CATM) and build a Git-
worktree environment for multi-turn agent RL.
In our setting, applying the efficiency signal
at the advantage layer, rather than the reward
layer, holds KL drift to one-third and translates
cleanly into downstream efficiency. We will
release the model, training pipeline, RL envi-
ronment, and evaluation harnesses.
1 Introduction
Modern LLM coding agents—general-purpose as-
sistants like Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025) and
open GitHub-issue-solving frameworks like Open-
Hands (Wang et al., 2024)—share a common in-
efficiency in how they allocate their token budget:
much of it is spentfindingthe file to patch, not writ-
ing the patch itself. In this work, we ground this
observation on a concrete instance: a 30B Open-
Hands agent on SWE-Bench Verified (Jimenez
et al., 2023) averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens
per resolved issue, with a large fraction consumed
bygrep,glob, andview_file calls issued in am-
biguous exploration loops—often 20+ rounds in a
wrong direction before the agent gives up.
Can a specialized retrieval submodule shorten
this exploration phase? Two hypotheses have not
been jointly tested.H1 (effectiveness): better file-
level retrieval steers the agent past dead-end ex-
plorations and raises the resolve rate.H2 (effi-
ciency): the agent resolves roughly the same set
of issues but with a shorter rollout. Distinguish-
ing them requires evaluating a retriever both on
its intrinsic quality and on its downstream effect
within the same agent stack—a comparison ab-
sent from prior open code retrievers, from lexical
(BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009)) to static
dense encoders (Feng et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2021;
Jina AI, 2024).

## Evidence locator: PDF Page 2

## PDF Page 2

Third, a systematic reward study across three
trained iterations (v1→v2→v3) yields two observa-
tions about GRPO reward design: in our setting,
applying an efficiency signal at the advantage layer
is markedly more stable than at the reward layer,
and removing an auxiliary component absent from
the downstream tool improves both training stabil-
ity and downstream efficiency (§3.5).
Contributions.
• CodeGrep, an open 14B agent-style code re-
triever trained end-to-end with GRPO; injected
into a frozen OpenHands agent, it cuts rounds
by 15% and tokens by 19% on resolved SWE-
Bench Verified instances while lifting resolve
rate by+1.2pp.
• Aprecision-thresholdcharacterisation of
retrieval–agent coupling: across three re-
trievers (BM25 0.375, Jina 0.445, CodeGrep
0.677), downstream utility exhibits three
regimes—hurts, neutral, buys efficiency (§5.1).
• A reward-design studyshowing that (i)
reward-layer multiplicative scaling of a tool-
call penalty triples GRPO policy drift vs.
advantage-layer scaling (KL 0.31 vs. 0.09);
(ii) in our final iteration, dropping an auxiliary
line-range component from the base reward im-
proves both training stability and downstream
efficiency (§3.5).
• Full open release: model, CATM pipeline, RL
environment, and all evaluation harnesses.
2 Related Work
Code retrieval for SWE-Bench-style agents.
Static retrievers—dense code encoders (Feng et al.,
2020; Guo et al., 2021, 2022; Jina AI, 2024) and
lexical baselines such as BM25 (Robertson and
Zaragoza, 2009)—struggle when issue vocabulary
does not overlap with the target code, a common
failure mode in GitHub bug reports (§4.2). Pipeline
systems such as Agentless (Xia et al., 2024), Moat-
less (Örwall, 2024), and SWE-Fixer (Xie et al.,
2025) pair lightweight retrieval with LLM-based
reranking, but keep the retrieval component non-
trainable.
Agent-style search and tool use.Building on Re-
Act (Yao et al., 2023) and Toolformer (Schick et al.,
2023), coding agents such as OpenHands (Wang
et al., 2024) and SWE-agent (Yang et al., 2024) op-
erate over rich tool interfaces at the cost of dozens
of sequential calls per issue. For search specifically,
Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025) and ReasonIR (Shao
et al., 2025) train LLMs to use search engines with
RL, but target indexed web corpora rather than
repository file systems.
Reinforcement learning for tool policies.
GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) has been adapted to
multi-turn tool use in ToRL (Li et al., 2025), RA-
GEN (Wang et al., 2025), and concurrent Cognition
SWE-grep (Pan et al., 2025). A recurring difficulty
is reward-length exploitation when the reward
mixes task accuracy with efficiency signals. Our
v1→v2→v3 study (§3.5) traces one manifestation
and its resolution: moving the efficiency signal
from the reward to the advantage layer.
Trajectory mining as supervision.Learning
“what is relevant” from past agent reads is be-
havioural supervision with a long history in clas-
sical IR. LRAT (Zhou et al., 2026) applied this
to web-search agents with one-to-one browse-
relevance pairs. CATM (§3.4) adapts the template
to code retrievers that emit multiple parallel reads
per turn, requiring one-to-many attribution and per-
trajectory aggregation (Table 4); our source data
are open-source OpenHands trajectories (Nebius
AI, 2025).
3 Method
3.1 System Overview
The system runs in two decoupled phases (Fig. 1).
Duringtraining, CodeGrep is optimized with
GRPO in a custom RL environment (§3.3) against
relevance labels mined by CATM (§3.4). During
inference, the trained CodeGrep takes the issue de-
scription, emits a short list of candidate files, and
those files are injected into the prompt of a frozen
OpenHands downstream agent. Only the retriever
is trained; the downstream agent is untouched, so
any downstream measurement (§4) is unambigu-
ously attributable to what the retriever contributes
to the prompt.
3.2 CodeGrep: The Retrieval Model
CodeGrep is a 14B-parameter retriever built on
Qwen3-14B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2025). It exposes
three read-only primitives— grep (regex search),
glob (path matching), and read (file contents)—
mirroring how a developer navigates an unfamiliar
codebase. At each turn it emits up to 8 tool calls
executed concurrently; observations are appended

ResKV: Reconstructing Omitted Attention Contributions for Fixed-Budget KV
Cache Compression
Yuhang Zhan, Lisi Chen, Shuo Shang
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
agooostoo@gmail.com, lchen012@e.ntu.edu.sg, jedi.shang@gmail.com
Abstract
KV cache compression is essential for efficient long-context
inference.Existingevictionmethodspermanentlydiscardun-
selectedtokensandconsequentlyremovetheiraggregatecon-
tribution to attention. Merging-based alternatives preserve
moreinformationbutcanperturbretainedkeysandvaluesthat
should remain exact. We observe that the information omit-
ted by cache eviction can be formulated as residual statistics
in both the numerator and denominator of softmax attention.
Basedonthisobservation,weproposeResKV,whichdivides
a fixed KV budget into an exact main cache and a compact
residualcachethatreconstructsthecontributionofomittedto-
kens. ResKV lets main-cache tokens and residual entries par-
ticipateinthesamesoftmaxnormalization,soresidualentries
restorebothattentionnumeratoranddenominatormassrather
thanactingasapost-hoccorrection.Aconstruction-timevali-
dationproxydeterminesresidualallocationforeachlayerand
KV head, while a decode-time dynamic gate adjusts residual
contributions for individual queries. Comprehensive evalua-
tions on LongBench and RULER, covering query-aware and
query-agnostic settings, multiple backbones, cache budgets,
and representative compression baselines, demonstrate broad
improvements under the same retained KV budget while pre-
serving the practical efficiency of compressed decoding, in-
cludingpeakmemoryusageandlong-contextdecodethrough-
put.
Introduction
Long-context large language models rely on a KV cache to
avoid recomputing past keys and values during autoregres-
sive generation. While this cache makes decode efficient,
it also grows linearly with the context length and quickly
becomes a dominant source of memory use and memory
traffic[Kwonetal.2023,Shengetal.2023,Liuetal.2024b,
Hooper et al. 2024]. This creates a central tension in long-
context inference: the model should retain enough historical
informationtoanswerfuturequeries,butthesystemcanonly
afford to keep a limited number of KV slots.
KV cache compression methods commonly address this
tension by deciding which tokens to keep. Eviction-based
methods score cached tokens, retain a subset as exact keys
andvalues,andpermanentlydiscardtherest[Liuetal.2023,
Zhangetal.2023,Adnanetal.2024,Lietal.2024,Orenetal.

At decode time, ResKV combines the exact main cache

than an external value update. ResKV further uses adaptive
residual control at two points. During cache construction, a
validation proxy selects the residual budget for each layer
and KV head only when residual entries improve held-out
attention-output reconstruction. During decode, a dynamic
gate scales the residual logits according to the sharpness of
the main-cache attention, allowing residual mass under dif-
fuse attention while protecting sharp retrieval peaks.
We evaluate ResKV across multiple long-context bench-
marks,backbones,andrepresentativecompressionbaselines.

tion; the latter compresses the cache without access to the
future query and therefore better matches realistic deploy-

on tasks that require distributed contextual evidence, with
negligible additional memory overhead and stable through-
put at long context lengths. Ablations further confirm the
roles of the validation proxy, dynamic gate, and shared soft-

213	8 Conclusion
214	We introduced SEDEM, a selective decompres-
215	sion framework for long-context question an-
216	swering. SEDEM stores context segments as
217	compact hidden-state memories, selects query-
218	relevant blocks, and decompresses only selected
219	blocks into decoder-compatible hidden states.
220	Across four long-context QA benchmarks, SE-
221	DEM achieves higher scores than the evaluated
222	compression baselines in both 1B and 3B same-
223	backbone settings, while reducing online time-
224	to-first-token and improving decoding throughput
225	relative to ICAE. Ablations show that direct mem-
226	ory conditioning is substantially weaker than se-
227	lective decompression, supporting the separation
228	between compact memory storage and decoder-
229	layer conditioning.
230	Limitations
231	This work has several limitations. First, our se-
232	lection loss is trained using block-level evidence
233	labels, which all four benchmarks provide. When
234	such labels are unavailable, SEDEM can still be
235	operated in the selector-disabled mode used in our
236	ablations, but this forgoes the efficiency gains of
237	top-Kselection. Learning selection from weaker
238	signals, such as distant or self-supervised evi-
239	dence, is left to future work.
240	Second, our same-backbone experiments use
241	Llama-3.2-1B and 3B; we have not evaluated
242	whether the same quality and efficiency margins
243	over compression baselines transfer to substan-
244	tially larger backbones, where full-context fine-
245	tuning may become a stronger reference. Third,
246	the extraction and injection layers are chosen em-
247	pirically. Although Appendix A.12 provides a di-
248	agnostic study, we do not propose a principled
249	procedure for selecting these layers on new back-
250	bone families. We also do not evaluate broader
251	long-context suites or substantially longer con-
252	texts, where the trade-off between evidence cov-
253	erage, selection budget, and decompression cost
254	may differ.
255	Fourth, with the 3B backbone, SEDEM re-
256	mains below the full-context fine-tuned reference
257	on MuSiQue. Our selection-budget analysis (Ta-
258	ble 5) shows thatKcontrols a quality–context
259	trade-off: larger budgets can recover additional ev-
260	idence on some datasets but process more posi-
261	tions above the injection layer, reducing the effi-
262	ciency margin. Adaptive or iterative selection that
263	variesKper query is a natural direction for future
264	work.
265	Finally, our latency results follow a fully on-
266	line protocol that includes segmentation, encod-
267	ing, compression, selection, and selective decom-
268	pression. Precomputing query-independent docu-
269	ment memories could further improve efficiency,
270	but this system-level optimization is not evaluated
271	here.
272	Potential Risks
273	SEDEM is an efficiency method for long-context
274	language-model inference. By reducing the cost of
275	processing long contexts, it could lower the barrier
276	to large-scale automated text generation, including
277	low-quality or misleading content. The method
278	also conditions generation on selected and recon-
279	structed memory blocks rather than the full con-
280	text; if selection fails or relevant evidence is omit-
281	ted, the decoder may produce incomplete or un-
282	supported answers. Because the selector is trained
283	from gold evidence annotations, any bias in those
284	annotations may propagate to which evidence the
285	decoder sees. These risks are not unique to SE-
286	DEM, but they should be considered when apply-
287	ing the method.

489	den states, and a lightweight compressor stores

491	inference time, a query-conditioned selector se-

506	cross-model use, where a smaller encoder con-
507	structs memories that are decompressed for use by
508	a larger decoder. This separates the cost of con-
509	text processing from the capacity used for answer
510	generation.

8 Conclusion
We introduced SEDEM, a selective decompres-
sion framework for long-context question an-
swering. SEDEM stores context segments as
compact hidden-state memories, selects query-
relevant blocks, and decompresses only selected
blocks into decoder-compatible hidden states.
Across four long-context QA benchmarks, SE-
DEM achieves higher scores than the evaluated
compression baselines in both 1B and 3B same-
backbone settings, while reducing online time-
to-first-token and improving decoding throughput
relative to ICAE. Ablations show that direct mem-
ory conditioning is substantially weaker than se-
lective decompression, supporting the separation
between compact memory storage and decoder-
layer conditioning.
Limitations
This work has several limitations. First, our se-
lection loss is trained using block-level evidence
labels, which all four benchmarks provide. When
such labels are unavailable, SEDEM can still be
operated in the selector-disabled mode used in our
ablations, but this forgoes the efficiency gains of
top-Kselection. Learning selection from weaker
signals, such as distant or self-supervised evi-
dence, is left to future work.
Second, our same-backbone experiments use
Llama-3.2-1B and 3B; we have not evaluated
whether the same quality and efficiency margins
over compression baselines transfer to substan-
tially larger backbones, where full-context fine-
tuning may become a stronger reference. Third,
the extraction and injection layers are chosen em-
pirically. Although Appendix A.12 provides a di-
agnostic study, we do not propose a principled
procedure for selecting these layers on new back-
bone families. We also do not evaluate broader
long-context suites or substantially longer con-
texts, where the trade-off between evidence cov-
erage, selection budget, and decompression cost
may differ.
Fourth, with the 3B backbone, SEDEM re-
mains below the full-context fine-tuned reference
on MuSiQue. Our selection-budget analysis (Ta-
ble 5) shows thatKcontrols a quality–context
trade-off: larger budgets can recover additional ev-
idence on some datasets but process more posi-
tions above the injection layer, reducing the effi-
ciency margin. Adaptive or iterative selection that
variesKper query is a natural direction for future
work.
Finally, our latency results follow a fully on-
line protocol that includes segmentation, encod-
ing, compression, selection, and selective decom-
pression. Precomputing query-independent docu-
ment memories could further improve efficiency,
but this system-level optimization is not evaluated
here.
Potential Risks
SEDEM is an efficiency method for long-context
language-model inference. By reducing the cost of
processing long contexts, it could lower the barrier
to large-scale automated text generation, including
low-quality or misleading content. The method
also conditions generation on selected and recon-
structed memory blocks rather than the full con-
text; if selection fails or relevant evidence is omit-
ted, the decoder may produce incomplete or un-
supported answers. Because the selector is trained
from gold evidence annotations, any bias in those
annotations may propagate to which evidence the
decoder sees. These risks are not unique to SE-
DEM, but they should be considered when apply-
ing the method.

compatible with an intermediate decoder layer. A
frozen LLM maps each context segment into hid-
den states, and a lightweight compressor stores
each segment as a compact memory block. At
inference time, a query-conditioned selector se-
lects relevant memory blocks. Only the selected
blocks are then expanded by a decompressor into
reconstructed hidden states and injected at an in-
termediate decoder layer. The decoder there-
fore avoids processing the full raw context, while
also avoiding direct generation from highly com-
pressed memory slots.
Three consequences follow from decoupling
storage from decoder conditioning. First, mem-
ory construction is query-independent, so mem-
ories can be reused across multiple queries over
the same context. Second, LLM computation
scales with the selection budget rather than the
full context length. Third, the design supports
cross-model use, where a smaller encoder con-
structs memories that are decompressed for use by
a larger decoder. This separates the cost of con-
text processing from the capacity used for answer
generation.
We evaluate SEDEM on 2WikiMultiHopQA,
MuSiQue, QASPER, and HotpotQA-Distractor.

152	Infrastructure

154	sors not only as intermediate computation results, but also

162	next discuss three representative scenarios.
163	Service Auto-ScalingTo accommodate fluctuating request
164	loads, LLM service providers dynamically scale serving in-

167	weights are loaded once during initialization, elastic LLM
168	serving requires repeatedly distributing large model weights
169	(often exceeding 100 GB) to newly launched instances. There-
170	fore, model weights become shared tensor states whose place-
171	ment and materialization directly affect scaling latency.

Modern LLM infrastructure increasingly manages tensors
not only as computation data, but also as persistent states
shared across distributed components. Existing systems op-

weight loading, KV cache management, and checkpoint syn-

across evolving LLM workloads. In this paper, we identify
tensor lifecycle management as a missing abstraction layer in
LLM infrastructure and propose Tensor-as-a-Service (TaaS),
which decouples tensor state management from computa-
tion logic. We design and buildTensorCast, a distributed
tensor management layer that provides first-class tensor ab-
stractions, programmable lifecycle primitives, and a runtime

mechanisms. This enables developers to write tensor manage-

model weight materialization, weight synchronization, KV
cache management, and programmable request routing. Our
results show thatTensorCastachieves competitive perfor-

enabling new cross-component optimization policies. A pro-

turn agent workloads.

Infrastructure
LLM training and serving workloads increasingly treat ten-

as persistent states that must be created, transferred, stored,
and transformed across system components. Representative
examples include model weights shared across serving in-
stances, KV caches reused across requests, and checkpoint
tensors synchronized across training and inference workers.

becomes a fundamental challenge in LLM infrastructure. We
next discuss three representative scenarios.

serving requires repeatedly distributing large model weights
(often exceeding 100 GB) to newly launched instances. There-
fore, model weights become shared tensor states whose place-

      "source_locator": "Section 3.6 (PDF Page 5); Table 5, PDF Page 12"

  "evaluation_context": "SWE-Bench Verified (500 instances); downstream agent is OpenHands with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (temperature 0, 100-round max).   "title": "ResKV: Reconstructing Omitted Attention Contributions for Fixed-Budget KV Cache Compression",
  "event_hint": "ResKV: a KV-cache compression method that splits a fixed KV budget into an exact main cache plus a compact residual cache whose entries participate in the same softmax normalization, reconstructing the attention mass of evicted tokens.",
  "problem": "KV-cache eviction methods permanently discard unselected tokens and so remove their aggregate contribution to attention (both numerator and denominator mass of softmax). Merging-based alternatives preserve more information but can perturb retained keys/values that should remain exact. Either way, quality drops sharply under tight cache budgets.",
  "mechanism": "ResKV divides a fixed KV budget into an exact main cache and a compact residual cache. Residual entries are not a post-hoc correction; they participate in the same softmax normalization as exact main-cache tokens, restoring both attention numerator and denominator mass. A construction-time validation proxy selects the residual budget per layer and KV head only when it improves held-out attention-output reconstruction, and a decode-time dynamic gate scales residual logits per query according to the sharpness of main-cache attention.",
  "evidence": [
    {
      "claim": "ResKV improves all 32 displayed LongBench configurations and 63 of 64 displayed RULER configurations under the same retained KV budget, with the clearest gains under tight cache budgets and on tasks requiring distributed contextual evidence.",
      "value": "32/32 LongBench and 63/64 RULER configs improved",
      "baseline": "H2O, SnapKV, TOVA, AdaKV (same retained KV budget)",
      "condition": "LongBench and RULER, multiple backbones and budgets",
      "source_locator": "Introduction, PDF Page 2"
    },
    {
      "claim": "On RULER-4K with LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct at 10% budget (query-aware), adding ResKV raises the H2O average from 33.49 to 48.17 (+14.68), and on the same baseline at 40% budget from 75.25 to 80.74.",
      "value": "33.49 to 48.17 (10% q-Aware); 75.25 to 80.74 (40% q-Aware)",
      "baseline": "H2O without ResKV",
      "condition": "RULER-4K, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, same KV budget",
      "source_locator": "Table 5, PDF Page 13"
    },
    {
      "claim": "The gains are largest at tight budgets and shrink as budget grows: SnapKV 10% q-Aware rises from 56.37 to 60.74 with ResKV, while at 40% q-Aware it moves from 82.66 to 83.31; TOVA 10% q-Aware rises from 61.75 to 65.10.",
      "value": "+4.37 (SnapKV 10%) vs +0.65 (SnapKV 40%); +3.35 (TOVA 10%)",
      "baseline": "SnapKV and TOVA without ResKV",
      "condition": "RULER-4K, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct",
      "source_locator": "Table 5, PDF Page 13"
    },
    {
      "claim": "ResKV keeps retained main-cache keys and values exact (no perturbation of selected entries), unlike merging-based methods that fold evicted states into retained entries.",
      "value": null,
      "baseline": "Merging-based methods (Ca, KVMerger, KeepKV, SemantiCache)",
      "condition": "Main-cache integrity",
      "source_locator": "Introduction / Related Work, PDF Pages 1-2"
    },
    {
      "claim": "ResKV preserves the practical efficiency of compressed decoding, including peak memory usage and long-context decode throughput, with negligible additional memory overhead and stable throughput at long context lengths.",
      "value": "negligible memory overhead; stable throughput",
      "baseline": "Underlying compression baseline",
      "condition": "Same retained KV budget",
      "source_locator": "Abstract (PDF Page 1) and Introduction, PDF Page 2"
    }
  ],
  "evaluation_context": "LongBench and RULER (4K and 32K context) benchmarks. Backbones: LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct. Both query-aware and query-agnostic construction, cache budgets 10/20/30/40%. Baselines: H2O, SnapKV, TOVA, AdaKV. RULER-4K full-cache reference averages 95.25 (LLaMA) and 93.57 (Qwen). ResKV is applied additively on top of each baseline.",
  "limitations": "Residual allocation is decided per layer and KV head (validation proxy) and gated per query, adding mechanism complexity. The reviewed evidence emphasizes quality (RULER/LongBench) and states efficiency is preserved, but the detailed peak-memory and decode-throughput table behind the efficiency claim is not in the reviewed front evidence. Results are reported for 7-8B-class backbones in the visible tables.",
  "project_relevance": "Relevant to compression/transfer/placement for KV cache. By reconstructing the attention mass of evicted tokens under a fixed budget, ResKV improves quality at the same cache size, which directly reduces the bytes that must be stored or transferred for a given quality level.     "All numeric quality comparisons are read from Tables 5-7 (RULER-4K LLaMA, RULER-4K Qwen, RULER-32K LLaMA) on PDF Pages 13-15.",
    "The efficiency claim is stated in the Abstract and Introduction but its supporting table is not in the reviewed evidence pack."
  ],
  "evidence_gaps": [
    {
      "question": "What are the quantitative peak-memory and long-context decode-throughput numbers showing ResKV preserves efficiency under the same KV budget?",
      "terms": ["peak memory", "decode throughput", "long context", "memory overhead", "efficiency", "ResKV"]
    }
  ],

{
  "title": "SeDeM: Selective Decompression of Hidden-State Memories for Long-Context Question Answering",
  "event_hint": "SeDeM: a long-context QA framework that stores context as compressed hidden-state memory blocks, selects query-relevant blocks, and decompresses only those into a decoder layer, beating compression baselines and, with a 3B backbone, exceeding full-context fine-tuning on three of four datasets while lowering TTFT vs ICAE.",
  "problem": "Long-context inference is costly: prefill self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length and the KV cache grows with processed tokens, while larger context windows do not guarantee reliable evidence use. Existing soft-compression methods use an LLM as compressor and rely on compact memory tokens both to preserve information and to condition the decoder, coupling storage and decoding.",
  "mechanism": "SeDeM decouples compact memory storage from decoder conditioning. A frozen LLM extracts hidden states from a chosen intermediate Transformer layer; a lightweight compressor stores each segment as a memory block; a query-conditioned selector (trained with block-level evidence supervision) picks relevant blocks; a decompressor expands only the selected blocks into hidden states compatible with an intermediate decoder layer. The decoder thus avoids both full-context processing and direct generation from highly compressed slots. Because memory construction is query-independent, memories are reusable across queries and support cross-model (small encoder, larger decoder) use.",
  "evidence": [
    {
      "claim": "On four long-context QA benchmarks SeDeM beats the evaluated compression baselines in both 1B and 3B same-backbone settings; with the 3B backbone it exceeds full-context fine-tuning on three datasets (2WikiMultiHopQA, QASPER, HotpotQA-Distractor).",
      "value": "3B SeDeM > full-context FT on 3 of 4 datasets",
      "baseline": "LongLLMLingua, HMT, ICAE, 500x, Activation Beacon; full-context fine-tuning reference",
      "condition": "Llama-3.2-1B and 3B backbones, F1/ROUGE-L",
      "source_locator": "Table 2, PDF Page 7"
    },
    {
      "claim": "Concrete 3B F1 scores: 2WikiMultiHopQA 67.25 (SeDeM) vs 62.50 (full-context FT) and 38.77 (ICAE); HotpotQA-Distractor 58.30 vs 36.73 (full-context FT); on MuSiQue SeDeM (21.85) remains below full-context FT (32.54).",
      "value": "2Wiki 67.25 vs 62.50; HotpotQA 58.30 vs 36.73; MuSiQue 21.85 vs 32.54",
      "baseline": "Full-context fine-tuned reference and ICAE",
      "condition": "Llama-3.2-3B-Base",
      "source_locator": "Table 2, PDF Page 7"
    },
    {
      "claim": "SeDeM reduces online time-to-first-token versus ICAE: averaged across the four datasets, 3B TTFT is 79.60 ms vs 195.76 ms (2.46x), and 1B TTFT is 46.56 ms vs 81.07 ms (1.74x); on QASPER 3B the speedup reaches 3.77x (96.50 ms vs 364.10 ms).",
      "value": "3B avg TTFT 2.46x faster; QASPER 3B 3.77x faster",
      "baseline": "ICAE",
      "condition": "Fully online protocol (includes compression, selection, decoder prefill)",
      "source_locator": "Table 3, PDF Page 7"
    },
    {
      "claim": "SeDeM also improves autoregressive decoding throughput versus ICAE: 3B avg 45.16 vs 41.17 Tok/s (1.10x) and 1B avg 77.78 vs 71.82 Tok/s (1.08x); early-exit query encoding reduces 3B selection latency from ~26 ms to ~13 ms.",
      "value": "3B 1.10x throughput; 1B 1.08x throughput",
      "baseline": "ICAE",
      "condition": "Same backbones",
      "source_locator": "Table 3 and Section 6.2, PDF Page 7"
    },
    {
      "claim": "SeDeM's added inference-active modules are 33.59M params (2.72% of the frozen 1B backbone) and 75.55M params (2.35% of the 3B backbone), excluding LoRA adapters.",
      "value": "2.72% (1B) and 2.35% (3B) param overhead",
      "baseline": "Frozen Llama-3.2 backbones (1.236B / 3.213B params)",
      "condition": "Inference-time active modules",
      "source_locator": "Table 9, PDF Page 16"
    }
  ],
  "evaluation_context": "Four long-context QA benchmarks: 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, QASPER, HotpotQA-Distractor (train/val splits reported in Table 7). Backbones Llama-3.2-1B-Base and 3B-Base (frozen + LoRA). Baselines: LongLLMLingua (hard), HMT/ICAE/500x (soft), Activation Beacon (KV/activation), plus frozen and full-context fine-tuned references. Metrics: token-level F1 and ROUGE-L. Efficiency measured by TTFT (ms) and throughput (Tok/s) under a fully online protocol. A cross-model row uses a 1B encoder with a 3B decoder (e.g., HotpotQA F1 44.39).",
  "limitations": "Explicitly stated by the authors: (1) the selector needs block-level evidence labels for training (all four benchmarks provide them); without labels, selector-disabled mode forgoes the efficiency gains of top-K selection. (2) Only Llama-3.2-1B and 3B are evaluated; transfer to substantially larger backbones is unverified. (3) Extraction and injection layers are chosen empirically, with no principled procedure for new backbone families. (4) With 3B, SeDeM stays below full-context FT on MuSiQue, and the selection budget K trades quality against context/efficiency. (5) Latency follows a fully online protocol; precomputing query-independent memories could improve efficiency but is not evaluated.",
  "project_relevance": "Relevant to compression/transfer/placement. SeDeM's query-independent memory construction makes compressed context reusable across multiple queries over the same context, and its selective decompression reduces both decode cost and TTFT. For cross-region or cross-session reuse, storing compact hidden-state memory blocks (rather than full KV) could lower bandwidth and storage cost while preserving QA quality, with the caveat that selection currently relies on evidence labels.",
  "primary_source_resolved": true,
  "quality_score": 88,
  "source_notes": [
    "All QA scores are from Table 2 and efficiency numbers from Table 3 (PDF Page 7).",
    "Parameter-overhead figures are from Table 9 (PDF Page 16).",
    "Limitations are transcribed from the explicit Limitations section (PDF Page 9)."
  ],
  "evidence_gaps": [],
  "_task": {
    "id": "955a6d7395de3c050094f0b3",
    "type": "fact_extraction",
    "entity_id": "bb5261deaff2c6e927cee1de",
    "input_digest": "16bbd864f14ae9a1c3aa3febf3ab70a9"
  }
}

{
  "title": "TensorCast: The Missing Tensor Management Layer in Large Language Model Infrastructure",
  "event_hint": "TensorCast: a distributed tensor-management layer (Tensor-as-a-Service) that decouples tensor lifecycle management from computation, integrated with vLLM and SGLang; a programmable routing policy improves median TTFT by up to 93.2% under highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads.",
  "problem": "LLM infrastructure increasingly manages tensors (model weights, KV caches, checkpoints) as persistent distributed states, but existing systems optimize each task (weight loading, KV management, checkpoint sync) by deeply coupling task-specific mechanisms with execution engines, networks, or storage. This creates isolated silos that prevent reuse and cross-component composition, so operators repeatedly reimplement similar lifecycle logic and cannot express optimizations that span multiple components (e.g., jointly balancing load and preserving KV locality).",
  "mechanism": "TensorCast proposes Tensor-as-a-Service (TaaS), decoupling tensor state management from computation. It provides first-class tensor abstractions, programmable lifecycle primitives (identify/place/materialize/transform/coordinate), and a runtime that separates tensor-management policies from execution mechanisms. Developers compose tensor-management programs via TensorCast APIs while transparently leveraging distributed execution and data movement; engine-specific state export/import is confined to an instance adaptor so callers evolve without modifying engines, transports, or storage.",
  "evidence": [
    {
      "claim": "A programmable request-routing policy implemented with TensorCast improves median TTFT by up to 93.2% under highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads.",
      "value": "up to 93.2% median TTFT improvement",
      "baseline": "Load-aware / cache-aware router policies",
      "condition": "Highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads",
      "source_locator": "Abstract (PDF Page 1)"
    },
    {
      "claim": "For high-cardinality KV management (Qwen3-32B, TP=2) with RDMA enabled, TensorCast achieves TTFT reductions of 60% to 87.5% (2.5x to 8x speedup), comparable to the state-of-the-art Mooncake KV backend; with RDMA disabled it significantly outperforms Mooncake.",
      "value": "60-87.5% TTFT reduction (2.5x-8x) with RDMA",
      "baseline": "Mooncake KV storage backend in SGLang",
      "condition": "Qwen3-32B TP=2, LongBench prompts (~16k/35k tokens), 100% cache-hit stress test",
      "source_locator": "Section 6.3, PDF Page 13 (Fig. 8)"

All 6 fact-extraction tasks are complete and validated. Each output JSON echoes the input `_task` verbatim, matches the source title exactly, has `primary_source_resolved: true`, and carries ≤5 evidence items grounded in the fulltext.

## Results: 6 titles + quality_scores

1. **Deep Agentic Search for Repository-Level Code Question Answering: An Empirical Study** — quality_score **88**
   - Semantic search 65.2% vs deep agentic 46.2% on SWE-QA (pooled, 4 models); <half the cost per correct answer; 41.8% of deep-agent failures at the planner→subagent hand-off.

2. **Towards Load-Aware Prefill Deflection for Disaggregated LLM Serving** (Kairos) — quality_score **84**
   - Prefill execution only 2–23% of P95 TTFT (rest is queue + KV transfer); up to 81% P95 TTFT reduction / 79% SLO-attainment gain over SOTA disaggregated schedulers; <1 ms routing on vLLM 0.18.1, 2P2D A100 cluster.

3. **CodeGrep: An RL-Trained Retrieval Agent for LLM Coding Agents** — quality_score **87**
   - Baseline 30B OpenHands = 23 rounds / 631K tokens per resolved issue; CodeGrep (14B, GRPO) lifts resolve 25.8%→27.0% with −15% rounds / −19% tokens; precision threshold BM25 0.375 (hurts) / Jina 0.445 (neutral) / CodeGrep 0.677 (buys).

4. **ResKV: Reconstructing Omitted Attention Contributions for Fixed-Budget KV Cache Compression** — quality_score **84**
   - Main-plus-residual cache with shared-softmax; improves 32/32 LongBench and 63/64 RULER configs; e.g. H2O 10% q-Aware RULER-4K 33.49→48.17; gains largest at tight budgets.

5. **SeDeM: Selective Decompression of Hidden-State Memories for Long-Context Question Answering** — quality_score **88**
   - Beats compression baselines in 1B/3B; 3B exceeds full-context FT on 3/4 datasets (2Wiki 67.25 vs 62.50; HotpotQA 58.30 vs 36.73); 3B TTFT 2.46× faster than ICAE; 2.35% param overhead.

6. **TensorCast: The Missing Tensor Management Layer in Large Language Model Infrastructure** — quality_score **84**
   - TaaS abstraction integrated with vLLM/SGLang; KV management 60–87.5% TTFT reduction (2.5–8×) comparable to Mooncake with RDMA, better without; weight sync 1.14–2.63×; programmable router up to 93.2% median TTFT improvement.

Honest scoring notes: papers whose headline speedup's exact baseline/condition wasn't in the reviewed front evidence (Kairos 81%, TensorCast 93.2%) and the efficiency-detail table not visible (ResKV) were scored 84 and given one targeted `evidence_gaps` entry each; the two with fully-visible results tables (Deep Agentic Search, SeDeM) and CodeGrep scored 87–88.
